questions.q: Per this lesson, what two dimensions is a deployment risk scored along?
options: Cost and duration
Likelihood and impact -- how probable a failure mode is, and how severe it would be if it happened
Popularity and complexity
Number of lines of Apex code and number of fields affected
questions.explain: A deployment risk assessment scores each potential failure mode on likelihood (how probable) and impact (how severe), which together turn a vague sense of risk into something comparable across changes.

questions.q: Why does this lesson say a declarative change's impact score should reflect how many users and processes touch the object it's deployed to?
options: Declarative changes never carry any real risk, so impact is always scored as zero
Only programmatic changes need an impact score at all
Impact should only be scored based on how many lines of configuration were changed
A Flow or validation rule on a widely-used object like Account or Opportunity can affect every user who touches that object the moment it's active, regardless of how simple the change looks to build
questions.explain: The lesson warns that a declarative change's blast radius depends on how widely used the object it touches is, not on how complex the change appears technically.

questions.q: According to this lesson, how should a completed risk assessment relate to the rollback plan?
options: They should be completely unrelated, separate documents
A rollback plan is only needed if the risk assessment found zero risks
The rollback plan should respond directly to the specific risks the assessment surfaced, not offer a generic answer that ignores the highest-scored risk
The risk assessment should be written only after the rollback plan is already finalized
questions.explain: The lesson is explicit that the rollback plan needs a real answer for whatever the assessment's highest-scored risk actually is -- a generic rollback statement that ignores the specific risk defeats the purpose of doing the assessment.

questions.q: Which of the following is named in this lesson as a Salesforce-specific risk factor a generic risk framework often misses?
options: Whether the deployment is scheduled close to a seasonal release upgrade weekend, where a failure would be hard to attribute to the right cause
The number of competitors in the customer's industry
The color scheme of the Lightning page layout
The customer's annual revenue
questions.explain: Seasonal release interaction is one of the Salesforce-specific risk factors this lesson adds to a generic risk framework, because a failure near an upgrade weekend is hard to attribute to the right cause.

questions.q: Per this lesson's checklist, why should two changes with different rollback stories never be scored as equally risky just because they look technically similar?
options: Because rollback story has nothing to do with actual risk
Because only code changes can ever have a rollback plan
Because a change with a clean, real rollback path is genuinely less risky than one with no real recovery path, even if the two changes look alike on the surface
Because risk scoring should ignore data-change irreversibility entirely
questions.explain: The lesson specifically warns against scoring two similar-looking changes identically when one has a real data-recovery path and the other doesn't -- the irreversibility of a potential failure is a core part of its actual risk.
